guideSummary.surfnerd: Anchor Point is Morocco's most legendary wave, a long right-hand point peeling along a rock shelf just outside Taghazout. Australians first surfed it in the 1960s, and it has been the center of surfing in the region ever since. From a steep take-off at the outside peak, the wave delivers a seemingly endless run of speed walls and cutback hooks, with hollow sections and plenty of room for high-performance surfing.

A sectiony line with multiple take-off spots keeps the wave fun for every ability level and every surfcraft.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Boilers is a right-hand point and reef that breaks over rock on the far west end of Cap Ghair, the first spot you reach heading south around the headland. It takes its name from the rusty hull of a ship sitting just underwater at the top of the point, whose boiler shows itself and gurgles away at low tide. The wave is a quick runner that follows the rocks with real speed and punch, and it sits inside the cluster of waves around Taghazout, where prevailing winter winds blow offshore.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Dar Bouazza is one of Morocco's few lefthanders, a point that wraps around the headland about 40 minutes south of Casablanca's Anfa neighborhood. It's the most famous left in the country, peeling with decent length from the take-off at L'Inter down to the final section by the old ship boiler known as La Bobine. The wave is usually fairly fat, offering cut-back sections rather than a wall to hit, but it can pack a punch and throws up rippable sections when it's on.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Doura is a fast, hollow right-hander breaking over sand near the Bou Regreg rivermouth in Rabat-Salé. It's one of eight spots split up by the angled groynes at the rivermouth, and it's the standout of the group, with nearby Brema, La Pointe and Salé's shorebreak far less impressive. Sometimes compared to a Moroccan Kirra, it changed after development works but still throws the occasional barrel, running fast, long and hollow once the swell has some size.
